title: Observability — eBPF Deep Dive
description: Kernel-level observability: every syscall, every flow, every block I/O, every policy hit — captured by BPF programs running inside the kernel itself. Headline row shows signal volume and the in-kernel CPU/RAM cost of capturing it.

panels.title: Kernel events/sec captured
panels.description: Total events per second captured directly from kernel BPF programs (Tetragon process/policy events + Hubble network flows). This is the raw signal volume the kernel sees — not log lines an agent has to ship.

panels.title: If this were Splunk — $/day ingest
panels.description: Bytes/event × Splunk Cloud's published $5/GB/day. Upper bound only — these events never leave the kernel unless a TracingPolicy matches.

panels.title: BPF CPU overhead (% of one core)
panels.description: Total CPU time spent inside Tetragon's BPF programs, expressed as a fraction of one core. eBPF runs in-kernel and is the cheapest observation point in the system — typical overhead is 1-3% of one core for hundreds of thousands of events/sec.

panels.title: BPF data-plane memory (MB)
panels.description: Memory used by Cilium's BPF maps + program text. The entire kernel-side data plane for routing + L7 policy + observability — fits in a few hundred MB. Compare to your Splunk forwarder's RSS.

options.content: **Why eBPF wins vs log-shipping:** every event above was observed in the kernel, filtered against active policies, and exported only when it mattered. Splunk's model is the inverse — agents tail logs, ship every line over the network, then a backend indexer parses them. You pay 4× for the same data: agent CPU, network bandwidth, indexer CPU, license/storage. And you still miss everything that never made it into a log — privilege use, file opens, syscall errors, in-pod traffic between containers. The dollar figure above is just the ingest tax; the visibility gap is what we actually fix.

panels.title: Events emitted/sec (Tetragon)
panels.description: Tetragon events that matched a policy and were forwarded — execve, capability use, file ops, network ops. Kernel-observed, filtered in-kernel, structured at emission.

panels.title: Ring buffer overrun (lost/sec)
panels.description: Events dropped because the kernel-to-userspace ring buffer overflowed. Sustained non-zero = need a bigger ring or lower event volume. Should be 0 in steady state.

panels.title: Tracing policies loaded
panels.description: Active Tetragon TracingPolicies. Each policy is a set of kprobes/uprobes/tracepoints with filters. More policies = deeper coverage; each adds a few KB of BPF program text.

panels.title: Process cache size
panels.description: Processes Tetragon is tracking. Each entry holds the binary, args, parent chain, container/pod identity, capabilities — so every event can be enriched at emission without a userspace lookup.

panels.title: Event flow — what the kernel is reporting
Events received from kernel vs exported (showing in-kernel filter)
panels.description: `received` = raw events from the BPF programs. `exported` = events that survived in-kernel + userspace filtering. The gap is what Splunk would have to ship and you would have to pay to index — and discard.

panels.title: Events by msg_op (13=EXECVE, 14=EXIT, 15=KPROBE, 16=TRACEPOINT, 23=TEST)
panels.description: The kind of event firing. EXECVE / EXIT chains let you reconstruct every process tree. KPROBE / TRACEPOINT are policy-defined: file opens, network ops, capability use — whatever you wrote a TracingPolicy for.

panels.title: Tetragon errors/sec
panels.description: Categories of internal errors (event cache misses, ringbuf full, exporter timeouts). Should trend to zero in steady state.

panels.title: Event handling latency (kernel-to-userspace)
panels.description: Distribution of how long Tetragon takes to handle each event end-to-end. Hot top of histogram = falling behind, you need more userspace workers.

panels.title: Block I/O latency — the kernel's view, not iostat's
Block read latency (ebpf_exporter — kernel block layer)
panels.description: Latency distribution of every block layer read, captured by a BPF kprobe on block_rq_issue/block_rq_complete. Bypasses iostat's averaging — you see the tail. ZFS performance forensics gold: split by operation + device label.

panels.title: Block write latency (ebpf_exporter — kernel block layer)
panels.description: Same as read latency but for writes. Tail latency here = fsync stalls = upper-layer app latency. ZIL/SLOG sizing decisions live in this heatmap.

panels.title: Network — Hubble's L3/L4/L7 eBPF view of every pod-to-pod flow
Flows processed/sec
panels.description: Every TCP/UDP/ICMP flow between pods, observed in-kernel via Cilium's eBPF datapath. No app cooperation needed. No sidecar. No log line on either end. Just the kernel.

panels.title: Network drops/sec — what NetworkPolicy enforced
panels.description: Packets dropped by Cilium's eBPF data plane, by reason. This IS the access log for in-cluster traffic — every deny was made by a BPF program running at line rate, with zero userspace involvement.

panels.title: TCP flags distribution — connection lifecycle visibility
panels.description: SYN/RST/FIN/ACK rate. SYN spikes = new connections. RST = connection reset (interesting — app crash? policy deny? network blip?). FIN = clean close. The shape of these curves tells you the kind of traffic you're dealing with, no app instrumentation required.

panels.title: Hubble events lost (ring buffer health)
panels.description: Hubble equivalent of the Tetragon ringbuf-lost stat. Sustained non-zero = Hubble ringbuf is overflowing under flow rate; tune `hubble.eventBufferCapacity`.

panels.title: ICMP rate (reachability probes + diagnostics)
panels.description: ICMP echo/unreachable/redirect rate. Useful for spotting Kubelet liveness-probe storms, ARP-equivalent in IPv6, and network-tier debugging.

panels.title: BPF program overhead — the cost of observation
Tetragon BPF program time/sec (top 10 by kernel CPU)
panels.description: Time the kernel spent executing each Tetragon BPF program, per second. This is the literal CPU cost of observability, measured by the kernel itself — no estimation, no sampling.

panels.title: BPF program runs/sec (top 10 by call frequency)
panels.description: How often each BPF program fires. Cross-reference with the time/sec panel to spot expensive hooks: high runs + low time = cheap; low runs + high time = needs tuning.

panels.title: Cilium BPF data plane — map pressure (sizing health)
BPF map pressure — fullness ratio (top 15 maps)
panels.description: Fullness ratio per BPF map. Approaching 1.0 = the map is about to start evicting entries (connection state, identity cache, NAT entries). Sustained near-full = sizing problem; pump `bpfMapSize` for the relevant map type.

options.content:
### Why this dashboard exists

Four kernel-level modules let Linux do things that used to require separate userspace agents stacked on top:

| Module | What it puts in the kernel | What it replaces |
|---|---|---|
| **ZFS** | COW filesystem, snapshots, send/recv, ARC, dedup, checksum-on-read | rsync + LVM + tar + nightly scrubs scheduled by cron |
| **WireGuard** | Routable encrypted tunnels in the network stack | OpenVPN / IPsec / strongSwan userspace daemons |
| **eBPF** | Programmable, verified hooks across syscall + net + block + LSM | tcpdump + strace + iostat + auditd, each as its own agent |
| **KVM** | Type-1-class hardware virtualization in `/dev/kvm` | Type-2 hypervisors with a host kernel they don't trust |

kldload images ship all four as kernel modules + their userspace tooling + the BPF programs that attach to the hooks, built once and running unchanged on every node. That's the whole machine: one image, one kernel build, one set of policies.

### What this dashboard is reading

| Layer | Producer | Where it's filtered | Wire format |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process events (`execve`, exit, parent chain) | Tetragon | In-kernel BPF (kprobe + TracingPolicy) | protobuf |
| Capability use + policy hits | Tetragon | In-kernel `cap_use` kprobe | protobuf |
| Network flows, L7, drops | Hubble (Cilium agent) | In-kernel cgroup + tc BPF | protobuf |
| Block I/O latency (per-request) | ebpf_exporter | In-kernel block tracepoints | Prometheus histogram |
| BPF runtime cost (CPU per program) | `bpftool prog show` | `bpf_stats_enabled` syscall | text → prom |

### How it works

- **Filter compiles into the kernel.** A TracingPolicy is a BPF program verified and loaded into the kprobe / tracepoint hook on the producing CPU. The decision "is this event interesting?" happens before the event leaves kernel memory. Drop-by-default; emit only what matches.
- **Sealed image, end to end.** Kernel, modules, BPF programs, and userspace agents are built together and shipped as one image. The producer of an event and its consumer are the same version on every node. Upgrade by re-imaging, not by chasing version compatibility matrixes.
- **Event format is protobuf at emission.** Hubble and Tetragon use protobuf as their on-the-wire format. Typed fields, no regex parsing on the way in, forward-compat across producer / consumer versions.
- **One BPF surface for multiple signals.** Cilium loads the kernel programs; Tetragon and Hubble attach through it; ebpf_exporter sits beside them. Same verifier, same maps API, same per-CPU ring buffer. Process, network, and storage signals come from one infrastructure.
- **Userspace is a relay.** The Cilium agent pulls already-filtered events from the kernel ring buffer and forwards them. No regex / no string-to-field conversion at this layer; the BPF program did it.

### About the `$/day` panel

The calculation is `(observed-event-bytes-in-window) × $5/GB`. Published per-GB ingest list price applied to every byte the kernel observed in the time window. If a TracingPolicy keeps the event stream small, the actual operational cost of routing the same data through a SIEM scales down proportionally. The panel makes the cost-of-source-volume visible at the point of capture.
